# UPDATE: Fleet Operations Layer

**From:** The AV Market Strategist <avmarketstrategist@substack.com>  
**Date:** 2026-11-19T16:15:04.000Z

---

👋 Hey everyone,
In July I published the first version of my deep dive on the AV fleet operations layer: who cleans, charges, repairs and recovers robotaxis, and who gets paid for it.
Four months later, a lot of that map has moved. Waymo borrowed money for the first time. Three demand platforms started describing the same financing plan. Taxi companies turned up as operators from Shenzhen to Doha to Munich. And I recorded more than a dozen Autonomy Insiders conversations with the people who run this layer, from Holo in Oslo to FlexDrive, Grab, Oro, and more.
So I rebuilt the file. It is now close to twice as long.
If you have not come across these before: the deep dives are the long-form files I keep current, so there is one document that is actually up to date instead of a pile of old posts. WeRide came first, then Pony.ai, then fleet operations. I update them whenever the picture changes materially.
What I changed this time
The size of the prize, quantified. Three people who work on this layer gave  independent estimates of how much of a robotaxi ride goes to operations. They use different bases and land in the same band, and it is a bigger share than most people would guess.
New section: who pays for the metal. Waymo took the first debt in its history in October. I explain why that matters more for the operators than for Waymo, why residual value keeps the cheapest capital out, and why three of the four demand platforms now describe the same bridge. The fourth says the opposite.
New section: the human layer. The remote operator ratio I published in February, rebuilt as a corridor with both bases shown, the depot cost line nobody adds to it, and the one number seven AV companies declined to give a US senator.
A new operator class. Taxi companies, from Shenzhen and Shanghai to Singapore, Doha and Munich. What they bring that a new entrant cannot buy quickly, and what they carry.
A third operator bench, around Pony.ai. City by city, in China and abroad, plus the one caveat that keeps the picture honest.
New profile: Verne. The first local operator in this piece that owns its fleet and has started to export.
New chapter: what robotaxi operators can learn from public transport. Holo and beti, and the four capabilities an operator needs once its own name is on the permit. A permit issued in Madrid in September suggests that question is closer than it looks.
The rulebook. California, Germany and France each regulate a different variable of this layer, and that decides which capability becomes a compliance asset in which market.
Every profile current. Moove’s new equity and Las Vegas, Element’s second city, Flexdrive’s new depot, Oro as a standalone company against Hertz’s Q3, Avis still without a second city, and Avomo’s Spanish permit.
The scorecard, updated in place, and what changed in my view. Five of the six variables I track have moved since July. One thing I expected in July now looks further away, and I explain why.
The weekly newsletter is free, and it stays free.
The deep dives are the part I keep for the readers who chose to support this work when they did not have to. If you are on the free list, this is exactly what a paid subscription funds: every living file kept current, the full analysis behind the numbers, and the conversations that go into them.
If you already support The AV Market Strategist, thank you. The updated file is live now.
Thanks for reading.
